item.research_question: How can rare-earth high-entropy oxides (RE-HEOs) be utilized for CO2 reduction and other applications?
item.material_system: Rare-earth high-entropy oxides (RE-HEOs), such as (Ce0.2Zr0.2La0.2Nd0.2Sm0.2)O2−δ and Ce0.5(LaPrSmY)0.5O2−y
item.processing_route: Anchoring method, including adsorption of rare-earth metal cations by negative functional groups on the surface of graphene oxide, refluxing for 4 h at 170 °C, and calcinating at temperatures over 500 °C
item.test_conditions: Photocatalytic conditions, high temperature and high pressure for thermal catalysis, and electrocatalytic conditions with an external electric field
key_findings: RE-HEOs demonstrated significant catalytic performance for CO2 conversion under photocatalytic conditions
Achieved a production of 14.4 mol CO kg−1 h−1 and 1.27 mol CH3OH kg−1 h−1 with high selectivity for CO and methanol
Fluorite RE-HEOs showed tunable bandgap range of 2.0–3.5 eV, making them suitable for photovoltaic and LED applications
RE-HEOs exhibited enhanced thermal shock resistance and oxidation durability, making them suitable for high-temperature applications

item.mechanism: The catalytic performance of RE-HEOs is linked to their defect chemistry, particularly the formation and stabilization of oxygen vacancies
item.limitations: Current synthesis methods are not scalable and energy-efficient, and the high cost of rare-earth elements is a potential barrier to commercialization
item.future_work: Development of advanced synthesis techniques, investigation of less commonly studied rare-earth elements, and exploration of hybrid systems integrating RE-HEOs with other functional materials

records.text: Paper card. Question: How can rare-earth high-entropy oxides (RE-HEOs) be utilized for CO2 reduction and other applications?. System: Rare-earth high-entropy oxides (RE-HEOs), such as (Ce0.2Zr0.2La0.2Nd0.2Sm0.2)O2−δ and Ce0.5(LaPrSmY)0.5O2−y. Processing: Anchoring method, including adsorption of rare-earth metal cations by negative functional groups on the surface of graphene oxide, refluxing for 4 h at 170 °C, and calcinating at temperatures over 500 °C. Test conditions: Photocatalytic conditions, high temperature and high pressure for thermal catalysis, and electrocatalytic conditions with an external electric field. Findings: RE-HEOs demonstrated significant catalytic performance for CO2 conversion under photocatalytic conditions; Achieved a production of 14.4 mol CO kg−1 h−1 and 1.27 mol CH3OH kg−1 h−1 with high selectivity for CO and methanol; Fluorite RE-HEOs showed tunable bandgap range of 2.0–3.5 eV, making them suitable for photovoltaic and LED applications; RE-HEOs exhibited enhanced thermal shock resistance and oxidation durability, making them suitable for high-temperature applications; High-entropy zirconate-based oxides maintained their structural integrity under high-radiation exposure and exhibited stable luminescent performance. Mechanism: The catalytic performance of RE-HEOs is linked to their defect chemistry, particularly the formation and stabilization of oxygen vacancies. Limitations: Current synthesis methods are not scalable and energy-efficient, and the high cost of rare-earth elements is a potential barrier to commercialization. Future work: Development of advanced synthesis techniques, investigation of less commonly studied rare-earth elements, and exploration of hybrid systems integrating RE-HEOs with other functional materials. Quote: "an inviting way to make carbon flow in the ecosystem"
